paragraphs: A very long time ago, a young man named Giovanni Guasconti came from the more southern part of Italy to study at the University of Padua. With only a few gold ducats in his pocket, Giovanni rented a high, gloomy room in an old building grand enough to have been a Paduan nobleman’s palace. In fact, above its entrance it displayed the coat of arms of a family that had long since died out. The young newcomer knew something of his country’s great poem. He remembered that Dante had depicted one of this family’s ancestors, perhaps even a resident of this very mansion, suffering the eternal agonies of his Inferno. These memories and associations, together with a young man’s natural tendency towards heartbreak when away from home for the first time, made Giovanni sigh deeply as he looked around the desolate, poorly furnished room.

“Holy Virgin, sir!” cried old Dame Lisabetta. Won over by the young man’s remarkable beauty, she was kindly trying to make the room look habitable. “What a sigh to come from a young man’s heart! Do you find this old mansion gloomy? For the love of Heaven, then, put your head out of the window, and you’ll see sunshine as bright as any you left behind in Naples.”

Guasconti automatically did as the old woman suggested, but could not quite agree that the sunshine in Padua was as cheerful as that of southern Italy. Such as it was, however, it fell on a garden beneath his window, nourishing a variety of plants that seemed to have been cultivated with extraordinary care.
“Is this garden part of the house?” Giovanni asked.

“Heaven forbid, sir, unless it produced better herbs for cooking than anything growing there now,” old Lisabetta answered. “No, that garden is cultivated by the very hands of Mr. Giacomo Rappaccini, the famous doctor. I’m certain his name has been heard as far away as Naples. They say he distils these plants into medicines as powerful as a magic charm. You can often see the doctor at work, and perhaps the young lady, his daughter, too, gathering the strange flowers that grow in the garden.”
The old woman had now done what she could to improve the room’s appearance. Entrusting the young man to the protection of the saints, she left.

Giovanni still found nothing better to do than look down into the garden beneath his window. From its appearance, he judged it to be one of those botanical gardens established in Padua earlier than anywhere else in Italy, or indeed the world. Or, quite possibly, it had once been the pleasure garden of a wealthy family. In its centre stood the ruin of a marble fountain, sculpted with exceptional skill, but so sadly shattered that its original design could no longer be traced among the jumble of fragments. Yet the water continued to gush and sparkle in the sunbeams as cheerfully as ever. A little gurgling sound rose to the young man’s window. It made him feel as though the fountain were an immortal spirit, singing its song endlessly, heedless of the changes around it. One century gave it a body of marble; another scattered that perishable ornament across the ground. Around the pool into which the water settled grew various plants that seemed to need plentiful moisture to nourish their gigantic leaves and, in some cases, their gorgeously magnificent flowers. One shrub in particular stood in a marble vase in the middle of the pool. It bore a profusion of purple blossoms, each with the lustre and richness of a gem. Together they made such a brilliant display that they seemed enough to light the garden even without sunshine. Every patch of soil was populated with plants and herbs. Those less beautiful still showed signs of painstaking care, as though each had its own special properties, known to the scientific mind that nurtured it. Some stood in urns richly decorated with old carvings, others in ordinary garden pots. Some crept like serpents along the ground or climbed high, using whatever support they could find. One plant had wound itself around a statue of Vertumnus, completely veiling and shrouding it in a drapery of hanging leaves. These were so beautifully arranged that they might have served as a model for a sculptor.

As Giovanni stood at the window, he heard a rustling behind a screen of leaves and realised that someone was working in the garden. The figure soon came into view. It was no ordinary labourer, but a tall, emaciated, sickly-looking man with a yellowish complexion, wearing the black clothes of a scholar. He was past middle age, with grey hair, a thin grey beard, and a face strikingly marked by intelligence and learning. Yet that face could never, even in his younger days, have expressed much warmth of heart.

Nothing could have exceeded the concentration with which this scientific gardener examined every shrub along his path. He seemed to be looking into their deepest nature, observing the essence of their creation, and discovering why one leaf grew in this shape and another in that, and why particular flowers differed in colour and scent. Yet despite his profound understanding, there was nothing approaching intimacy between him and these living plants. On the contrary, he avoided touching them or directly breathing in their scents with a caution that made a deeply unpleasant impression on Giovanni. The man behaved like someone walking among hostile powers—savage beasts, deadly snakes, or evil spirits—which would inflict some terrible death on him if he gave them a moment’s freedom. The sight of a man tending a garden with such a sense of danger filled the young man’s imagination with a strange fear. Gardening was the simplest and most innocent of human tasks, both the joy and the labour of humanity’s first parents before their fall. Was this garden, then, the Eden of the present world? And was this man, so conscious of danger in what his own hands had grown, its Adam?

The wary gardener protected his hands with thick gloves as he picked off dead leaves or pruned the shrubs’ excessive growth. Nor was this his only armour. When his walk through the garden brought him to the magnificent plant that hung its purple gems beside the marble fountain, he put a kind of mask over his mouth and nostrils, as though all that beauty concealed an even deadlier malice. But finding the task still too dangerous, he drew back, took off the mask, and called loudly, though in the weak voice of someone suffering from an internal illness, “Beatrice! Beatrice!”

“Here I am, Father. What would you like?” called a rich, youthful voice from a window of the opposite house. It was as rich as a tropical sunset, and made Giovanni think, though he did not know why, of deep purple and crimson colours and heavy, delicious perfumes. “Are you in the garden?”
“Yes, Beatrice,” the gardener replied, “and I need your help.”

Soon a young girl emerged beneath a carved doorway. She was dressed as richly and tastefully as the most splendid flowers, beautiful as the day, with colouring so deep and vivid that one shade more would have been too much. She seemed overflowing with life, health and energy. In all their abundance, these qualities seemed bound down and compressed, tightly encircled by the belt at her maidenly waist. Yet Giovanni’s imagination must have grown morbid as he looked down into the garden. The beautiful stranger struck him as another flower, the human sister of those plants, as beautiful as they were—more beautiful than the richest of them—but still to be touched only with a glove and approached only with a mask. As Beatrice came down the garden path, she could be seen touching and breathing in the scent of several plants her father had most carefully avoided.

“Here, Beatrice,” her father said, “see how much necessary care our chief treasure requires. Yet in my broken state of health, I might pay with my life for approaching it as closely as the work demands. From now on, I fear, this plant must be left entirely in your care.”

“And I will gladly take it on,” the young lady cried again in her rich voice, bending towards the magnificent plant and opening her arms as though to embrace it. “Yes, my sister, my splendour, it will be Beatrice’s task to nurse and serve you. And you will reward her with your kisses and your perfumed breath, which is like the breath of life to her.”

Then, with all the tenderness in her manner that her words had expressed so strikingly, she busied herself giving the plant whatever care it seemed to need. At his high window, Giovanni rubbed his eyes. He almost doubted whether he was seeing a girl tending her favourite flower or one sister showing loving care for another. The scene soon ended. Whether Dr. Rappaccini had finished his work in the garden or his watchful eye had caught sight of the stranger’s face, he now took his daughter’s arm and withdrew. Night was already closing in. Oppressive fumes seemed to rise from the plants and drift upwards past the open window. Giovanni closed the latticed window, went to bed, and dreamed of a rich flower and a beautiful girl. Flower and maiden were different, yet the same, and filled with some strange danger in either form.

But morning light has an influence that tends to correct whatever errors of imagination, or even judgement, we may have fallen into as the sun sets, among the shadows of night, or in the less wholesome glow of moonlight. Giovanni’s first movement on waking was to throw open the window and gaze into the garden that his dreams had made so fertile with mysteries. He was surprised and a little ashamed to find how real and ordinary it looked. The first rays of sunshine gilded the dewdrops on leaf and blossom, giving each rare flower a brighter beauty while bringing everything within the bounds of ordinary experience. The young man rejoiced that, in the heart of the barren city, he had the privilege of overlooking this lovely, luxuriant patch of vegetation. He told himself it would serve as a symbolic language to keep him in communion with Nature. True, neither the sickly Dr. Giacomo Rappaccini, worn down by thought, nor his brilliant daughter was now visible. Giovanni therefore could not tell how much of the strangeness he attributed to them came from their own qualities and how much from his wonder-working imagination. But he was inclined to take a thoroughly rational view of the whole affair.

During the day he paid a respectful visit to Mr. Pietro Baglioni, professor of medicine at the university, a highly distinguished physician for whom Giovanni had brought a letter of introduction. The professor was an elderly man, apparently good-natured, with habits that might almost be called jovial. He invited the young man to stay for dinner. His free, lively conversation made him very agreeable company, especially when he was warmed by a flask or two of Tuscan wine. Giovanni assumed that men of science living in the same city must know one another well, and took an opportunity to mention Dr. Rappaccini. But the professor’s response was less friendly than he had expected.

“It would be unbecoming for a teacher of the divine art of medicine,” Professor Pietro Baglioni said in answer to a question from Giovanni, “to withhold deserved and carefully considered praise from a physician as highly skilled as Rappaccini. Yet my conscience would hardly excuse me if I allowed a worthy young man like you, Mr. Giovanni, the son of an old friend, to absorb mistaken ideas about someone who might one day hold your life and death in his hands. The truth is that our honoured Dr. Rappaccini knows as much science as any member of the medical profession in Padua, or all Italy—with perhaps one single exception. But there are certain serious objections to his professional character.”
“And what might those be?” the young man asked.

“Does my friend Giovanni have some illness of the body or the heart, to make him so curious about physicians?” the professor asked with a smile. “But as for Rappaccini, people say—and I know the man well and can vouch for its truth—that he cares infinitely more for science than for humanity. His patients interest him only as subjects for some new experiment. He would sacrifice human life, including his own, or whatever else was dearest to him, simply to add so much as a mustard seed to the great heap of knowledge he has accumulated.”

“He sounds like a frightening man indeed,” Guasconti remarked, recalling Rappaccini’s cold, purely intellectual appearance. “And yet, honoured professor, isn’t there a noble spirit in that? Are many men capable of so spiritual a love of science?”

“God forbid,” the professor answered rather irritably, “at least unless they have sounder views of the art of healing than Rappaccini does. His theory is that all healing powers are contained in the substances we call plant poisons. He grows these with his own hands. He is even said to have produced new kinds of poison, more horribly harmful than any with which Nature would have plagued the world without this learned man’s help. It is undeniable that the doctor does less harm than one might expect with such dangerous substances. Now and then, we must admit, he has achieved—or seemed to achieve—a marvellous cure. But to tell you my private opinion, Mr. Giovanni, he deserves little credit for such successes, which are probably the work of chance. He should, however, be held strictly responsible for his failures, which can justly be considered his own work.”

The young man might have taken Baglioni’s opinions with many grains of salt had he known about the long-running professional warfare between him and Dr. Rappaccini. Rappaccini was generally thought to have gained the advantage in that struggle. Any reader wishing to judge for themselves may consult certain pamphlets in Gothic type, written on both sides and preserved in the medical department of the University of Padua.

“I don’t know, most learned professor,” Giovanni replied, after reflecting on what had been said about Rappaccini’s devotion to science alone. “I don’t know how dearly this physician loves his art, but surely one thing is dearer to him. He has a daughter.”

“Aha!” the professor cried with a laugh. “So now our friend Giovanni’s secret is out. You’ve heard of this daughter, whom all the young men in Padua are wild about, though not even half a dozen have ever been lucky enough to see her face. I know little of the young lady Beatrice, except that Rappaccini is said to have taught her his science in great depth. Young and beautiful as she is reported to be, she is already qualified to hold a professorship. Perhaps her father intends her to take mine! There are other absurd rumours, not worth discussing or listening to. So now, Mr. Giovanni, finish your glass of Lachryma wine.”

Guasconti returned to his lodgings somewhat warmed by the wine he had drunk. It had left his head swimming with strange imaginings about Dr. Rappaccini and the beautiful Beatrice. On the way, he happened to pass a florist’s and bought a fresh bouquet of flowers.

Going up to his room, he sat near the window, but in the shadow cast by the depth of the wall, so that he could look down into the garden with little risk of being discovered. Everything beneath him was deserted. The strange plants basked in the sunshine, occasionally nodding gently to one another as though acknowledging their sympathy and kinship. In their midst, beside the shattered fountain, grew the magnificent shrub, covered in clusters of purple gems. They glowed in the air and shone back from the depths of the pool, which seemed to overflow with coloured radiance from the rich reflection steeped in it. At first, as we have said, the garden was deserted. Soon, however, as Giovanni had half hoped and half feared, a figure appeared beneath the old carved doorway. She came down between the rows of plants, breathing in their various perfumes as though she were one of those beings from ancient classical myth who lived on sweet scents. Seeing Beatrice again, the young man was startled by how much her beauty exceeded his memory of it. It was so brilliant, so vivid, that she glowed amid the sunlight and, as Giovanni whispered to himself, actually lit up the shadowier stretches of the garden path. Her face was more clearly visible than before. He was struck by its expression of simplicity and sweetness, qualities he had not imagined in her character, and which made him ask again what kind of mortal she could be. Once more, too, he noticed—or imagined—a likeness between the beautiful girl and the gorgeous shrub hanging its gemlike flowers over the fountain. Beatrice seemed whimsically to have heightened this resemblance, both in the arrangement of her dress and in her choice of its colours.

As she approached the shrub, she flung open her arms with what seemed passionate fervour and drew its branches into an intimate embrace. It was so close an embrace that her face disappeared into its leafy breast, and her shining ringlets mingled with the flowers.

“Give me your breath, my sister,” Beatrice exclaimed, “for ordinary air makes me faint. And give me this flower of yours, which I remove from its stem with the gentlest fingers and place close beside my heart.”

With these words, Rappaccini’s beautiful daughter picked one of the shrub’s richest blossoms and was about to fasten it at the breast of her dress. But now, unless the wine Giovanni had drunk had confused his senses, a strange incident occurred. A small orange-coloured reptile, a kind of lizard or chameleon, happened to be creeping along the path just at Beatrice’s feet. It appeared to Giovanni—though at that distance he could scarcely have seen anything so tiny—it appeared to him, nevertheless, that a drop or two of moisture fell from the flower’s broken stem onto the lizard’s head. For an instant the reptile twisted violently, then lay motionless in the sunshine. Beatrice noticed this remarkable event and crossed herself sadly, but without surprise. Even so, she did not hesitate to arrange the deadly flower at her breast. There it blushed, almost glimmering with the dazzling effect of a precious stone, adding to her dress and appearance the one fitting charm that nothing else in the world could have supplied. But Giovanni leaned forwards out of his window’s shadow, then shrank back, murmuring and trembling.
“Am I awake? Do I still have my senses?” he said to himself. “What is this being? Should I call her beautiful, or terrible beyond words?”

Beatrice now wandered casually through the garden, drawing closer beneath Giovanni’s window. To satisfy the intense and painful curiosity she aroused, he had to push his head right out of its hiding place. At that moment, a beautiful insect came over the garden wall. Perhaps it had wandered through the city, finding neither flowers nor greenery among those ancient human dwellings, until the heavy perfumes of Dr. Rappaccini’s shrubs had lured it from afar. Without settling on the flowers, this winged brightness seemed drawn to Beatrice, hovering in the air and fluttering around her head. Now, surely Giovanni Guasconti’s eyes must have been deceiving him. However that might be, it seemed to him that, while Beatrice watched the insect with childish delight, it grew faint and fell at her feet. Its bright wings shivered. It was dead, from no cause he could detect unless it was the air she breathed out. Once again Beatrice crossed herself, and sighed deeply as she bent over the dead insect.

An impulsive movement from Giovanni drew her eyes to the window. There she saw the young man’s beautiful head, more Greek than Italian, with fair, regular features and a glint of gold among his ringlets. He gazed down at her like a being hovering in mid-air. Hardly knowing what he was doing, Giovanni threw down the bouquet he had been holding.
“Madam,” he said, “here are pure, wholesome flowers. Wear them for Giovanni Guasconti’s sake.”

“Thank you, sir,” Beatrice replied. Her rich voice poured out like a rush of music, and her joyful expression was half a child’s and half a woman’s. “I accept your gift, and would gladly repay it with this precious purple flower. But if I throw it into the air, it won’t reach you. So Mr. Guasconti must be satisfied with my thanks.”

She picked up the bouquet, then hurried homewards through the garden, as though privately ashamed that she had put aside her maidenly reserve to answer a stranger’s greeting. But brief as those moments were, when she was about to disappear beneath the carved doorway, Giovanni thought his beautiful bouquet was already beginning to wither in her hand. It was a foolish thought. At such a distance, it would have been impossible to tell a faded flower from a fresh one.

For many days after this incident, the young man avoided the window overlooking Dr. Rappaccini’s garden, as though some ugly, monstrous thing would have blasted his sight if he had been tempted into a glance. He was aware that, by opening communication with Beatrice, he had placed himself to some extent under a power he could not understand. If his heart was in any real danger, the wisest course would have been to leave his lodgings, and Padua itself, at once. The next wisest would have been to accustom himself, as far as possible, to seeing Beatrice in the familiar light of day, bringing her firmly and systematically within the bounds of ordinary experience. Above all, he should not have avoided seeing this extraordinary being while remaining so close to her. Her nearness, and even the possibility of contact, gave a kind of substance and reality to the wild fantasies his imagination continually ran riot in producing. Guasconti did not have a deep heart—or, at any rate, its depths were not being reached now. But he had a lively imagination and a passionate southern temperament that rose every moment to a higher fever pitch. Whether or not Beatrice possessed the terrible qualities suggested by what Giovanni had witnessed—that deadly breath, that kinship with the beautiful and deadly flowers—she had at least introduced a fierce, subtle poison into his system. It was not love, although her rich beauty drove him mad. Nor was it horror, even when he imagined her spirit filled with the same harmful essence that seemed to run through her body. It was a wild offspring of love and horror, with something of each parent in it, burning like one and shivering like the other. Giovanni did not know what to dread, and still less what to hope for. Yet hope and dread fought constantly in his breast, defeating one another in turn and rising again to renew the struggle. Blessed are all simple emotions, whether dark or bright! It is the lurid mixture of the two that produces the illuminating blaze of hell.

Sometimes he tried to calm his fevered spirit by walking quickly through the streets of Padua or beyond its gates. His footsteps kept time with the throbbing in his brain, so that his walk tended to quicken into a run. One day he found himself stopped. A stout man had seized his arm, having turned back on recognising him and spent a great deal of breath catching up.
“Mr. Giovanni! Stop, my young friend!” he cried. “Have you forgotten me? You might well have done if I had changed as much as you.”

It was Baglioni, whom Giovanni had avoided ever since their first meeting, fearing that the professor’s sharp understanding might see too deeply into his secrets. Trying to collect himself, he stared wildly out of his inner world into the world around him and spoke like a man in a dream.
“Yes, I am Giovanni Guasconti. You are Professor Pietro Baglioni. Now let me pass!”

“Not yet, not yet, Mr. Giovanni Guasconti,” said the professor, smiling while he studied the young man with a serious, searching look. “What! Did I grow up side by side with your father, only for his son to pass me like a stranger in these old streets of Padua? Stand still, Mr. Giovanni. We must exchange a word or two before we part.”
“Quickly, then, most honoured professor, quickly,” Giovanni said with feverish impatience. “Can’t you see, sir, that I’m in a hurry?”

While he was speaking, a man dressed in black came along the street, stooping and moving weakly like someone in poor health. His entire face had a sickly, yellowish colour. Yet its expression revealed such a piercing, active intelligence that an observer might easily have overlooked the merely physical features and seen only that extraordinary energy. As he passed, he exchanged a cold, distant greeting with Baglioni, but fixed his eyes on Giovanni with an intensity that seemed to draw out everything in him worth noticing. Nevertheless, there was a peculiar calmness in the look, as though he took only an intellectual, rather than a human, interest in the young man.
“It is Dr. Rappaccini!” the professor whispered after the stranger had passed. “Has he ever seen your face before?”
“Not that I know of,” Giovanni answered, starting at the name.

“He HAS seen you! He must have seen you!” Baglioni said quickly. “For some purpose or other, this man of science is studying you. I know that look of his! It casts the same cold light over his face when he bends over a bird, a mouse, or a butterfly that he has killed with a flower’s scent as part of an experiment. It is a look as deep as Nature itself, but without Nature’s loving warmth. Mr. Giovanni, I will stake my life on it: you are the subject of one of Rappaccini’s experiments!”
“Are you trying to make a fool of me?” Giovanni cried passionately. “THAT, Professor, would be an ill-judged experiment.”

“Patience! Patience!” replied the professor, entirely unruffled. “I tell you, my poor Giovanni, that Rappaccini has a scientific interest in you. You have fallen into terrible hands! And the young lady Beatrice—what part does she play in this mystery?”

But Guasconti found Baglioni’s persistence unbearable. He broke away and was gone before the professor could seize his arm again. Baglioni watched the young man intently as he went, and shook his head.

“This must not happen,” Baglioni said to himself. “The young man is my old friend’s son, and he shall suffer no harm that the secrets of medical science can protect him from. Besides, it is intolerably insolent of Rappaccini to snatch the lad out of my own hands, so to speak, and use him for his infernal experiments. This daughter of his! I shall look into it. Perhaps, most learned Rappaccini, I may thwart you where you least expect it!”

Meanwhile Giovanni had taken a roundabout route and eventually found himself at the door of his lodgings. As he crossed the threshold, old Lisabetta met him, smirking and smiling, plainly trying to attract his attention. Her efforts were useless, however, for his boiling emotions had momentarily subsided into a cold, dull emptiness. He looked straight at her withered face as it puckered into a smile, but seemed not to see it. The old woman therefore grasped his cloak.

“Sir! Sir!” she whispered, still smiling across the whole breadth of her face, so that it looked rather like a grotesque wooden carving darkened by centuries. “Listen, sir! There is a private entrance into the garden!”
“What are you saying?” Giovanni exclaimed, turning quickly, as though a lifeless object had suddenly sprung into feverish life. “A private entrance into Dr. Rappaccini’s garden?”

“Hush! Hush! Not so loud!” Lisabetta whispered, putting her hand over his mouth. “Yes, into the honoured doctor’s garden, where you can see all his fine shrubs. Many a young man in Padua would pay gold to be allowed among those flowers.”
Giovanni placed a gold coin in her hand.
“Show me the way,” he said.

A suspicion crossed his mind, probably prompted by his conversation with Baglioni. Perhaps old Lisabetta’s intervention was connected with the intrigue, whatever its nature, in which the professor seemed to believe Dr. Rappaccini was involving him. But although the suspicion disturbed Giovanni, it was not enough to hold him back. The moment he knew it was possible to approach Beatrice, doing so seemed essential to his very existence. It did not matter whether she was an angel or a demon. He was irrevocably within her sphere and had to obey the law that whirled him onwards in ever-smaller circles towards an outcome he did not try to foresee. Yet, strangely, he suddenly wondered whether his intense interest might itself be a delusion. Was it really deep and definite enough to justify thrusting himself into a situation whose consequences he could not calculate? Was it merely a fantasy in a young man’s brain, with little or no connection to his heart?

He paused, hesitated, half turned back, then went on again. His withered guide led him along several dim passages and finally unfastened a door. As it opened, he saw and heard rustling leaves, with patches of sunlight glimmering among them. Giovanni stepped out and pushed through the tangle of a shrub whose tendrils curled over the hidden entrance. He stood beneath his own window, in the open space of Dr. Rappaccini’s garden.

How often, when impossible things have happened and dreams have condensed their misty substance into solid reality, do we find ourselves calm, even coldly self-possessed! We stand among circumstances whose prospect would have driven us into a frenzy of joy or agony. Fate delights in frustrating us this way. Passion chooses his own moment to rush onto the scene, and lingers sluggishly behind when events seem perfectly arranged to summon him. So it was now with Giovanni. Day after day, his feverish blood had pounded at the unlikely thought of meeting Beatrice and standing face to face with her in this very garden. He had imagined basking in the eastern sunshine of her beauty and snatching from her direct gaze the mystery he believed was the riddle of his own existence. Yet now there was a strange, ill-timed calm in his breast. He glanced around the garden to see whether Beatrice or her father was there. Finding himself alone, he began to examine the plants critically.

The appearance of every one of them displeased him. Their splendour seemed fierce, passionate, even unnatural. There was scarcely a shrub that would not have startled someone wandering alone through a forest if he had found it growing wild, as though an unearthly face had glared at him out of the thicket. Several would also have shocked a sensitive observer with their artificial appearance. It suggested such mixing—almost adultery—between different plant species that the result was no longer God’s creation, but the monstrous offspring of man’s corrupt imagination, glowing with only an evil mockery of beauty. They were probably the results of experiments that, in one or two cases, had combined individually lovely plants into something with the same dubious, threatening character as everything else growing in the garden. In short, Giovanni recognised only two or three plants in the collection, and those were kinds he knew well to be poisonous. While occupied with these thoughts, he heard the rustle of a silk garment. Turning, he saw Beatrice emerge from beneath the carved doorway.

Giovanni had not thought about how he should behave. Should he apologise for intruding into the garden? Or should he assume that Dr. Rappaccini or his daughter at least knew he was there, perhaps even wanted him there? Beatrice’s manner put him at ease, though it still left him uncertain who had arranged his admission. She came lightly along the path and met him near the broken fountain. There was surprise in her face, brightened by a simple, kind expression of pleasure.

“You are a fine judge of flowers, sir,” Beatrice said with a smile, referring to the bouquet he had thrown her from the window. “It is no wonder, then, that the sight of my father’s rare collection has tempted you to look more closely. If he were here, he could tell you many strange and interesting facts about the nature and habits of these shrubs. He has spent a lifetime studying them, and this garden is his world.”

“And you yourself, lady,” Giovanni said, “if what people say is true, are also deeply knowledgeable about the properties suggested by these rich blossoms and spicy scents. If you would consent to teach me, I should learn more readily than if Mr. Rappaccini himself were my teacher.”

“Are there such idle rumours?” Beatrice asked, her pleasant laugh sounding like music. “Do people say I understand my father’s science of plants? What a joke! No, although I have grown up among these flowers, I know nothing about them beyond their colours and their scent. Sometimes I wish I could rid myself even of that little knowledge. There are many flowers here, and not the least brilliant ones, that shock and offend me when I see them. But please, sir, do not believe these stories about my scientific knowledge. Believe nothing about me except what you see with your own eyes.”

“And must I believe everything I have seen with my own eyes?” Giovanni asked pointedly, shrinking as he remembered earlier scenes. “No, madam, you ask too little of me. Tell me to believe nothing except what comes from your own lips.”
It seemed that Beatrice understood him. A deep blush rose in her cheek, but she looked straight into Giovanni’s eyes and met his gaze of uneasy suspicion with the proud disdain of a queen.

“Then that is what I ask you to do, sir,” she replied. “Forget whatever you may have imagined about me. Even if it was true to what your senses could detect, it may still be false in its essence. But the words from Beatrice Rappaccini’s lips are true from the depths of the heart outwards. Those you may believe.”

Her whole appearance glowed with feeling, shining into Giovanni’s mind like the light of truth itself. But as she spoke, a fragrance hung in the air around her, rich and delightful, though fleeting. An unexplained reluctance made the young man scarcely dare to draw it into his lungs. It might be the scent of the flowers. Could it be Beatrice’s breath that embalmed her words with such strange richness, as though steeping them in her heart? A faintness passed over Giovanni like a shadow and flitted away. He seemed to look through the beautiful girl’s eyes into her transparent soul, and felt no more doubt or fear.

The touch of passion that had coloured Beatrice’s manner vanished. She grew cheerful and seemed to take a pure delight in talking with the young man, rather as a girl on a lonely island might have felt while speaking with a traveller from the civilised world. Evidently, her experience of life had been confined to that garden. Sometimes she talked of things as simple as daylight or summer clouds. At other times she asked about the city, or Giovanni’s distant home, his friends, his mother, and his sisters. Her questions revealed such seclusion and such unfamiliarity with customs and manners that Giovanni answered as though speaking to an infant. Her spirit poured out before him like a fresh little stream catching its first glimpse of sunlight and wondering at the reflections of earth and sky cast into its breast. Thoughts came from a deep source too, and imaginings of jewel-like brilliance, as though diamonds and rubies sparkled upwards among the bubbles of the fountain. Now and then, wonder flashed across the young man’s mind. He was walking beside the very being who had so powerfully worked on his imagination, whose image he had painted in such colours of terror, and whose dreadful qualities he had actually seen revealed. He was talking with Beatrice like a brother, and finding her so human and so girlish. But these reflections lasted only a moment. Her character made such a real impression that it felt familiar at once.

Talking freely like this, they had wandered through the garden. After many turns along its paths, they now came to the shattered fountain, beside which grew the magnificent shrub with its treasury of glowing blossoms. A fragrance spread from it that Giovanni recognised as identical to the one he had attributed to Beatrice’s breath, but incomparably stronger. As her eyes fell on it, Giovanni saw her press a hand to her breast, as though her heart had suddenly begun to beat painfully.
“For the first time in my life,” she murmured to the shrub, “I had forgotten you.”

“I remember, madam,” Giovanni said, “that you once promised to reward me with one of these living gems for the bouquet I gladly dared to toss at your feet. Allow me to pick it now as a keepsake of this meeting.”

He stepped towards the shrub with his hand outstretched. But Beatrice darted forward with a shriek that pierced his heart like a dagger. She caught his hand and pulled it back with all the strength in her slender body. Giovanni felt her touch thrill through every fibre of him.
“Don’t touch it!” she cried in a voice of agony. “Not if you value your life! It is deadly!”

Then, hiding her face, she fled from him and vanished beneath the carved doorway. Following her with his eyes, Giovanni saw the wasted figure and pale, intelligent face of Dr. Rappaccini. He had been watching the scene from the shadow of the entrance, for how long Giovanni did not know.

As soon as Guasconti was alone in his room, Beatrice’s image returned to his passionate thoughts. It carried all the enchantment that had gathered around it since he first saw her, and now also the tender warmth of her young womanhood. She was human. Her nature possessed every gentle, feminine quality. She was supremely worthy of worship, and surely capable, herself, of the heights and heroism of love. The signs he had previously regarded as proof of some frightening peculiarity in her physical and moral nature were now either forgotten or transformed by passion’s subtle, deceptive reasoning into a golden crown of enchantment. The more unique Beatrice was, the more admirable this made her. Everything that had seemed ugly was now beautiful. Whatever could not be changed in this way slipped off and hid among the shapeless half-ideas crowding the dim region beyond the daylight of our full consciousness. He spent the night like this and did not fall asleep until dawn had begun to wake the sleeping flowers in Dr. Rappaccini’s garden, where Giovanni’s dreams no doubt led him. The sun rose at its proper time and cast its beams on the young man’s eyelids, waking him to a sense of pain. When fully awake, he became aware of a burning, tingling agony in his hand—in his right hand—the very hand Beatrice had grasped when he was about to pick one of the jewel-like flowers. On the back of that hand was now a purple print like four small fingers, and on his wrist the shape of a slender thumb.

Oh, how stubbornly love—or even that deceptive imitation of love that flourishes in the imagination but takes no deep root in the heart—how stubbornly it holds to its faith until the moment when it is doomed to vanish into thin mist! Giovanni wrapped a handkerchief around his hand and wondered what evil thing had stung him. Soon he forgot his pain in a daydream of Beatrice.

After the first meeting, the inevitable course of what we call fate brought a second. A third followed, then a fourth. A meeting with Beatrice in the garden was no longer an incident in Giovanni’s daily life. It was the whole stretch of time in which he could be said to live, for the rest consisted of anticipating and remembering that ecstatic hour. It was the same for Rappaccini’s daughter. She watched for the young man’s arrival and flew to his side with confidence as complete and open as though they had been playmates since earliest infancy—as though they were playmates still. If, on some unusual occasion, he failed to come at the arranged time, she stood beneath his window and sent up the rich sweetness of her voice to float around him in his room and echo and resound throughout his heart. “Giovanni! Giovanni! Why are you taking so long? Come down!” And down he hurried into that Eden of poisonous flowers.

But despite all this closeness, Beatrice still maintained a reserve so strict and unchanging that the idea of violating it scarcely entered his mind. By every visible sign, they loved each other. Their eyes had spoken love, carrying the holy secret from the depths of one soul into the depths of the other, as though it were too sacred to whisper in passing. They had even spoken of love in those outpourings of passion when their spirits leapt out in spoken breath like tongues of long-hidden flame. Yet they had not sealed their love with a kiss, nor clasped hands, nor shared even the slightest caress of the kind love claims and makes sacred. He had never touched a single gleaming curl of her hair. So marked was the physical barrier between them that a breeze had never even blown her dress against him. On the few occasions when Giovanni seemed tempted to cross the boundary, Beatrice became so sad and stern, and her face showed such desolate isolation, as though shuddering at that very isolation, that no spoken word was needed to drive him back. At such times he was startled by the horrible suspicions that rose like monsters from the caverns of his heart and stared him in the face. His love grew thin and faint as morning mist; only his doubts had substance. But when Beatrice’s face brightened again after that momentary shadow, she was immediately transformed from the mysterious, questionable being he had watched with such awe and horror. She was once more the beautiful, unworldly girl whom he felt his spirit knew with a certainty beyond all other knowledge.

A considerable time had now passed since Giovanni’s last meeting with Baglioni. One morning, however, he was unpleasantly surprised by a visit from the professor, whom he had scarcely thought about for weeks and would gladly have forgotten for longer still. He had long surrendered himself to an all-consuming excitement. He could tolerate companions only if they were entirely in sympathy with his present feelings. Such sympathy could not be expected from Professor Baglioni.
The visitor chatted casually for a few moments about gossip from the city and the university, then turned to another subject.

“I have been reading an old classical author lately,” he said, “and came across a story that I found strangely interesting. Perhaps you remember it. It concerns an Indian prince who sent a beautiful woman as a gift to Alexander the Great. She was as lovely as the dawn and as gorgeous as the sunset. But what particularly distinguished her was a certain rich perfume in her breath—richer than a garden of Persian roses. Alexander, as was natural for a young conqueror, fell in love at first sight with this magnificent stranger. But a certain wise physician who happened to be present discovered a terrible secret about her.”
“And what was that?” Giovanni asked, lowering his eyes to avoid the professor’s gaze.

“That this lovely woman,” Baglioni continued emphatically, “had been fed on poisons from birth, until her whole nature was so saturated with them that she herself had become the deadliest poison in existence. Poison was the very substance of her life. With the rich perfume of her breath, she poisoned the very air. Her love would have been poison—her embrace, death. Isn’t that an extraordinary tale?”
“A childish fable,” Giovanni answered, springing nervously from his chair. “I wonder how you find time, sir, to read such nonsense among your more serious studies.”

“By the way,” said the professor, looking uneasily around him, “what is this strange fragrance in your room? Is it the perfume of your gloves? It is faint but delicious, and yet, all things considered, not pleasant at all. If I breathed it for long, I think it would make me ill. It is like the breath of a flower, but I see no flowers in the room.”

“There aren’t any,” replied Giovanni, who had turned pale while the professor spoke. “Nor do I think there is any fragrance, except in your imagination, sir. Scents are made of something both physical and spiritual, and so they can deceive us in this way. The memory of a perfume, the mere idea of it, can easily be mistaken for something actually present.”

“Yes, but my sober imagination does not often play such tricks,” Baglioni said. “And if I imagined any sort of smell, it would be that of some foul medicine, the kind of substance quite likely to cling to my fingers. Our esteemed friend Rappaccini, I have heard, scents his medicines with perfumes richer than those of Araby. No doubt the beautiful and learned young lady Beatrice would likewise treat her patients with doses as sweet as a young woman’s breath. But disaster awaits the man who takes a sip!”

Many conflicting emotions showed on Giovanni’s face. The professor’s tone when he referred to Rappaccini’s pure and lovely daughter tortured his soul. Yet the suggestion of a view of her character opposite to his own instantly gave clear shape to a thousand dim suspicions, which now grinned at him like so many demons. He struggled hard, however, to suppress them and answer Baglioni with a true lover’s perfect faith.

“Professor,” he said, “you were my father’s friend. Perhaps you also mean to act as a friend to his son. I would like to feel nothing towards you except respect and deference. But I ask you to understand, sir, that there is one subject we must not discuss. You do not know the young lady Beatrice. You therefore cannot judge the wrong—the blasphemy, I might even say—that a flippant or insulting word does to her character.”

“Giovanni! My poor Giovanni!” the professor answered, with a calm expression of pity. “I know this wretched girl far better than you do. You shall hear the truth about the poisoner Rappaccini and his poisonous daughter—yes, as poisonous as she is beautiful. Listen, for even if you strike this grey head of mine, it will not silence me. Through Rappaccini’s profound and deadly science, that old fable of the Indian woman has come true in the person of the lovely Beatrice.”
Giovanni groaned and hid his face.

“Her father,” Baglioni continued, “was not held back by natural affection from sacrificing his child in this horrible way to his insane passion for science. For, to do him justice, he is as true a scientist as ever distilled his own heart in a distillation flask. What, then, will your fate be? Without a doubt, you have been chosen as the material for some new experiment. Perhaps the outcome will be death; perhaps a fate more terrible still. With what he calls the interests of science to guide him, Rappaccini will stop at nothing.”
“It is a dream,” Giovanni muttered to himself. “Surely it is a dream.”

“But take heart, son of my friend,” the professor continued. “It is not yet too late for a rescue. Perhaps we may even succeed in bringing this miserable child back within the bounds of ordinary nature, from which her father’s madness has separated her. Look at this little silver vase! It was made by the hands of the renowned Benvenuto Cellini and is well worthy of being a lover’s gift to the most beautiful lady in Italy. But its contents are beyond price. One little sip of this antidote would have made the Borgias’ most powerful poisons harmless. Do not doubt that it will be just as effective against Rappaccini’s. Give the vase, and the precious liquid inside it, to your Beatrice, and wait hopefully for the result.”
Baglioni placed a small, exquisitely crafted silver vial on the table and left, allowing his words to work on the young man’s mind.

“We will foil Rappaccini yet,” he thought, chuckling to himself as he went down the stairs. “But let us admit the truth about him: he is a remarkable man—a remarkable man indeed. In his practice, however, he is a vile quack, and therefore cannot be tolerated by those who respect the good old rules of the medical profession.”

Throughout his acquaintance with Beatrice, Giovanni had occasionally been haunted, as we have said, by dark suspicions about her character. Yet she had made him feel so strongly that she was a simple, natural, deeply affectionate and innocent creature that Professor Baglioni’s picture of her seemed strange and incredible—as though it did not agree with Giovanni’s own first impression. True, there were ugly memories connected with his earliest glimpses of the beautiful girl. He could not quite forget the bouquet that had withered in her grasp, or the insect that had died in the sunny air, with no visible cause except the fragrance of her breath. But those incidents had dissolved in the pure light of her character. They no longer carried the force of facts and were accepted as mistaken fancies, whatever evidence of the senses might seem to support them. Something exists that is truer and more real than what we can see with our eyes or touch with a finger. Giovanni had based his confidence in Beatrice on that better evidence, though the irresistible force of her noble qualities had done more to establish it than any deep and generous faith of his own. Now, however, his spirit could no longer sustain itself at the height to which the first enthusiasm of passion had raised it. He fell, grovelling among earthly doubts, and stained the pure whiteness of Beatrice’s image with them. He had not given her up; he merely distrusted her. He decided to make a decisive test that would satisfy him once and for all. Did those dreadful peculiarities really exist in her physical nature—peculiarities that could not be supposed to exist without some corresponding monstrosity in her soul? Looking down from far above, his eyes might have deceived him about the lizard, the insect and the flowers. But if, from only a few paces away, he could see a fresh, healthy flower suddenly wither in Beatrice’s hand, there could be no further question. With this in mind, he hurried to the florist’s and bought a bouquet still jewelled with the morning’s dewdrops.

It was now the usual hour for his daily meeting with Beatrice. Before going down into the garden, Giovanni did not fail to look at himself in the mirror. Such vanity was to be expected in a beautiful young man. But to display it at that troubled, feverish moment revealed a certain shallowness of feeling and insincerity of character. He did look, however, and told himself that his features had never shown such rich grace, his eyes such liveliness, or his cheeks such a warm colour of overflowing life.
“At least,” he thought, “her poison has not yet crept into my system. I am no flower to die in her grasp.”

At that thought, he looked at the bouquet, which he had never once put down. A rush of indefinable horror shot through his body as he saw that the dewy flowers were already beginning to droop. They looked like things that had been fresh and lovely yesterday. Giovanni turned white as marble and stood motionless before the mirror, staring at his own reflection as though it were the image of something frightful. He remembered Baglioni’s remark about the fragrance that seemed to fill the room. It must have been the poison in his breath! Then he shuddered—shuddered at himself. Recovering from his daze, he began to watch with curiosity a spider busy hanging its web from the room’s old ceiling moulding. It crossed and recrossed its ingenious network of interwoven threads, as vigorous and active a spider as ever dangled from an old ceiling. Giovanni bent towards the insect and let out a deep, long breath. The spider suddenly stopped its work. The web vibrated with a tremor that began in the little craftsman’s body. Again Giovanni let out a breath, deeper, longer, and filled with a venomous feeling from his heart. He did not know whether he was wicked or merely desperate. The spider clutched convulsively with its legs and hung dead across the window.
“Cursed! Cursed!” Giovanni muttered, addressing himself. “Have you become so poisonous that your breath kills this deadly insect?”
At that moment, a rich, sweet voice came drifting up from the garden.
“Giovanni! Giovanni! It is past the hour! Why are you taking so long? Come down!”
“Yes,” Giovanni muttered again. “She is the only being my breath might not kill! I wish it could!”

He rushed down and in an instant stood before Beatrice’s bright and loving eyes. A moment earlier, his anger and despair had been so fierce that he could have wished for nothing more than to wither her with a glance. But her actual presence brought influences too real to be shaken off at once. He remembered the gentle and kindly power of her feminine nature, which had so often surrounded him with a religious calm. He remembered the many holy and passionate outpourings of her heart, when its pure fountain had been opened from its depths and revealed in all its transparency to his mind’s eye. Had Giovanni known how to value these memories, they would have assured him that all this ugly mystery was only an earthly illusion. They would also have assured him that, whatever mist of evil might seem to have gathered over her, the real Beatrice was a heavenly angel. Though he was incapable of such lofty faith, her presence had not entirely lost its magic. His rage subsided into an appearance of sullen numbness. Beatrice, with her quick spiritual awareness, immediately sensed a gulf of blackness between them that neither could cross. They walked on together, sad and silent, until they reached the marble fountain and its pool of water on the ground. In the middle of it grew the shrub with the gem-like blossoms. Giovanni was frightened by the eager enjoyment—the appetite, as it were—with which he found himself breathing in the flowers’ fragrance.
“Beatrice,” he asked abruptly, “where did this shrub come from?”
“My father created it,” she answered simply.
“Created it! Created it!” Giovanni repeated. “What do you mean, Beatrice?”

“He has a terrifying knowledge of Nature’s secrets,” Beatrice replied. “And at the hour when I first drew breath, this plant sprang from the soil, the offspring of his science and intellect, while I was only his earthly child. Do not go near it!” she continued, seeing with terror that Giovanni was moving closer to the shrub. “It has qualities you can scarcely imagine. But I, dearest Giovanni—I grew up and blossomed with the plant and was nourished by its breath. It was my sister, and I loved it with a human affection. For, sadly—haven’t you suspected it?—there was a terrible fate.”
At this, Giovanni frowned at her so darkly that Beatrice stopped and trembled. But her faith in his tenderness reassured her, and she blushed at having doubted it for a moment.

“There was a terrible fate,” she continued, “the result of my father’s fatal love of science, which cut me off from all company of my own kind. Until Heaven sent you, dearest Giovanni, oh, how lonely your poor Beatrice was!”
“Was it a hard fate?” Giovanni asked, fixing his eyes on her.
“Only recently have I understood how hard it was,” she answered tenderly. “Oh, yes—but my heart was dormant, and so it was quiet.”
Giovanni’s rage burst out of his sullen gloom like a flash of lightning from a dark cloud.

“Cursed creature!” he cried, with venomous scorn and anger. “And because you grew tired of your solitude, you have cut me off as well from all the warmth of life and lured me into your realm of unspeakable horror!”
“Giovanni!” Beatrice exclaimed, turning her large, bright eyes towards his face. The force of his words had not yet reached her understanding. She was simply thunderstruck.

“Yes, you poisonous thing!” Giovanni repeated, beside himself with passion. “You have done it! You have blighted me! You have filled my veins with poison! You have made me a creature as hateful, as ugly, as loathsome and deadly as yourself—a hideous monstrosity for the whole world to marvel at! Now, if we are lucky and our breath is as fatal to ourselves as to everyone else, let us join our lips in one kiss of unspeakable hatred, and die!”
“What has happened to me?” Beatrice murmured, with a low moan from her heart. “Holy Virgin, pity me, a poor, heartbroken child!”

“You—are you praying?” Giovanni cried, still with the same devilish scorn. “Your very prayers poison the air with death as they leave your lips. Yes, yes; let us pray! Let us go to church and dip our fingers in the holy water at the entrance! Those who follow us will die as if a plague had struck them! Let us trace crosses in the air! That will scatter curses everywhere in the form of holy symbols!”

“Giovanni,” Beatrice said calmly, for her grief had gone beyond passion, “why do you link yourself with me in those terrible words? I am indeed the horrible thing you call me. But you—what do you have to do except give one more shudder at my hideous misery, leave the garden, mix with your fellow humans, and forget that such a monster as poor Beatrice ever crawled upon the earth?”
“Are you pretending not to know?” Giovanni asked, scowling at her. “Look! This is the power I have gained from Rappaccini’s pure daughter.”

A swarm of summer insects flitted through the air, searching for the food promised by the flowers’ scents in the deadly garden. They circled Giovanni’s head, clearly attracted to him by the same influence that had briefly drawn them within range of several of the shrubs. He breathed out among them and smiled bitterly at Beatrice as at least twenty of the insects fell dead to the ground.

“I see it! I see it!” Beatrice shrieked. “It is my father’s deadly science! No, no, Giovanni; I did not do it! Never! Never! I dreamed only of loving you and being with you for a little while, then letting you go, leaving just your image in my heart. For, Giovanni, believe this: though my body is nourished by poison, my spirit is God’s creature and craves love as its daily food. But my father—he has joined us in this terrible bond. Yes; reject me, trample on me, kill me! Oh, what is death after words like yours? But I did not do it. I would not have done it for a whole world of bliss.”

Giovanni’s passion had exhausted itself in the outburst from his lips. Now he felt, mournfully and not without tenderness, the intimate and peculiar relationship between Beatrice and himself. They stood, as it were, in complete solitude, which even the densest crowd of human beings would make no less lonely. Should not the desert of humanity around them press this isolated pair closer together? If they were cruel to each other, who was there to be kind to them? Besides, Giovanni thought, might there still be hope of returning within the bounds of ordinary nature and leading Beatrice—the redeemed Beatrice—by the hand? O weak, selfish, unworthy spirit, to dream that an earthly union and earthly happiness were possible after such deep love had been so bitterly wronged as Beatrice’s love had been by Giovanni’s blighting words! No, no; there could be no such hope. She must make her heavy way, with that broken heart, beyond the boundaries of Time. She must bathe her wounds in some fountain of paradise, forget her grief in the light of immortality, and be well THERE.
But Giovanni did not know this.

“Dear Beatrice,” he said, approaching her. She shrank away as she always did when he came near, but now for a different reason. “Dearest Beatrice, our fate is not yet so hopeless. Look! There is a medicine, powerful, as a wise physician has assured me, and almost divine in its effects. It is made from ingredients utterly opposed to those with which your dreadful father has brought this calamity upon you and me. It is distilled from blessed herbs. Shall we drink it together, and so be purified of evil?”

“Give it to me!” Beatrice said, holding out her hand to receive the little silver vial that Giovanni drew from inside his clothes at his chest. She added, with a peculiar emphasis, “I will drink, but you must wait for the result.”

She put Baglioni’s antidote to her lips. At that same moment, Rappaccini’s figure emerged from the doorway and moved slowly towards the marble fountain. As he approached, the pale man of science seemed to gaze triumphantly at the beautiful young man and woman. He was like an artist who had spent his life creating a painting or a group of statues and was finally satisfied with his success. He stopped. He straightened his bent body, conscious of his own power. He spread his hands over them like a father pleading for a blessing upon his children. But those were the very hands that had poured poison into the stream of their lives. Giovanni trembled. Beatrice shuddered nervously and pressed her hand to her heart.

“My daughter,” Rappaccini said, “you are no longer lonely in the world. Pick one of those precious gems from your sister shrub and tell your bridegroom to wear it at his breast. It will not harm him now. My science and the bond between you and him have worked so deeply within his body that he now stands apart from ordinary men, just as you, daughter of my pride and triumph, stand apart from ordinary women. Go on, then, through the world, most precious to one another and terrifying to everyone else!”
“My father,” Beatrice said weakly, keeping her hand upon her heart as she spoke, “why did you inflict this miserable fate upon your child?”

“Miserable!” Rappaccini exclaimed. “What do you mean, foolish girl? Do you think it is misery to possess marvellous gifts against which no enemy’s power or strength can do anything? Misery, to be able to overpower the mightiest with a breath? Misery, to be as terrifying as you are beautiful? Would you have preferred to be a weak woman, exposed to every evil and capable of none?”

“I would rather have been loved than feared,” Beatrice murmured, sinking to the ground. “But now it does not matter. I am going, Father, where the evil you have tried to mingle with my being will pass away like a dream—like the fragrance of these poisonous flowers. Their scent will no longer taint my breath among the flowers of Eden. Farewell, Giovanni! Your words of hatred are like lead in my heart, but they too will fall away as I ascend. Oh, was there not more poison in your nature than in mine from the very beginning?”

Rappaccini’s skill had altered Beatrice’s earthly body so completely that, just as poison had been life to her, the powerful antidote was death. And so the poor victim of human ingenuity, of nature forced from its course, and of the fatal doom that accompanies all such efforts of corrupted wisdom died there, at the feet of her father and Giovanni. At that very moment, Professor Pietro Baglioni looked out of the window and called loudly, in a tone of triumph mixed with horror, to the thunderstruck man of science: “Rappaccini! Rappaccini! And is this the outcome of your experiment!”
